abstract: Significance The dysregulation of the p38α MAPK pathway is often linked to abnormal cell inflammation, death, and proliferation, contributing to tumorigenesis. Posttranslational modifications (PTMs) play a pivotal role in regulating p38α activation, yet their precise mechanisms are not fully understood. The present study revealed that KDM5D demethylates p38α at K165, which inhibits p38α phosphorylation, thereby slowing the tumor progression. Further, the present findings suggest that the methylation status of p38α at K165 could be a potential biomarker in clinical settings. These findings not only establish a crucial PTM-based regulatory mechanism for p38α but also suggest that targeting KDM5D can serve as a unique therapeutic approach for NSCLC.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Cell Lines and Cell Culture.
The HEK293T, A549, and BEAS-2B (a human bronchial epithelial cell line) were cultured at 37 °C in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 50 mg/mL penicillin/streptomycin in a humidified incubator with 5% CO
2
. The NCI-H1299, NCI-H1373, and NCI-H1573 cells were cultured at 37 °C in 1640 complete medium containing 10% FBS and 50 mg/mL penicillin/streptomycin. These cells were used within 10 to 15 passages. Cell culture reagents and other chemicals were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Gibco & Hyclone) and Sigma-Aldrich.
Reagents and Antibodies.
Most biochemical reagents were purchased from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). All the special reagents and antibodies can be found in
SI Appendix
.
Plasmid Constructs and Transfection.
The lentiviruses for CRISPR/Cas9-based editing of KDM5D were generated as previously described (
22
). All plasmids were sequenced and confirmed for accuracy. More details were found in
SI Appendix
. The sequences of PCR primers for Expressing Vectors used in this study are listed in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
.
Survival Analysis and Gene Expression Analysis.
KDM5D expression data were obtained from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (
7
,
24
,
25
). Additionally, for survival analysis, a publicly accessible transcriptomic dataset for lung cancer was utilized (
https://kmplot.com/analysis
) (
7
,
26
,
27
).
Mass Spectrometry Analyses.
For mass spectrometry analysis aimed at identifying methylation sites, anti-Flag IPs were conducted using whole cell lysates (WCLs) obtained from three 10-cm dishes of HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-p38α. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated via SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. All gel bands were excised and subjected to reverse-phase nanospray liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (Analytical Instrumentation Center of PEKING University, Beijing, China).
LC–MS/MS analysis was conducted to identify proteins interacting with p38α. A co-IP was performed using WCLs from HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-p38α or an empty vector control. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE, and Coomassie staining was used for visualization. All the gel bands were excised and subsequently subjected to LC–MS/MS (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
B
) (Beijing Protein Innovation, China). Additionally, LC–MS/MS was employed to identify proteins interacting with KDM5D. Co-IP was performed using WCLs in HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-KDM5D or an empty vector control. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and subjected to Coomassie staining. All bands were excised and subjected to LC–MS/MS (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
D
) (Beijing Protein Innovation, China).
qRT-PCR Analysis.
Total RNA was isolated using the RNAeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen). After quantifying using a Nanodrop 1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific), one microgram of total RNA was reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA with a Superscript III kit (Invitrogen). Real-time PCR was performed using the Power SYBR green PCR master mix (Takara). All analyses were performed using an Applied Biosystems® 7500 Fast PCR machine. mRNA was normalized by GAPDH. Each experiment was performed in triplicate.
Western Blot and Immunoprecipitation.
Methods of western blot and IP were described in
SI Appendix
.
Colony Formation Assays.
Cells were seeded into 6-well plates (500 cells/well) and incubated for 8 to 14 d until visible colonies formed. The colonies were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and fixed with 4% PFA for 20 min, then stained with 0.4% crystal violet in 20% ethanol for 30 min. After staining, the plates were washed, air-dried, and the number of colonies was counted. The control or KDM5D-deficient cells were treated with the p38α MAPK inhibitor SB203580 (10 μM, Selleck, cat # S1076) for 12 h prior to the colony formation assay.
Transwell Migration Assay.
A total of 5 × 10
4
cells were seeded on the porous membrane of each insert for the transwell migration assay. A more detailed method was described in
SI Appendix
.
Wound-Healing Assay.
A total of 7 × 10
5
A549 cells or 5 × 10
5
NCI-H1299 cells were seeded in a well of a 6-well plate, and a more detailed method was described in
SI Appendix
.
IHC staining.
This study was granted approval from the Institutional Review Board at the First Affiliated Hospital of Henan University. Informed consent was duly obtained from all patients who participated in this study. Paired fresh cancerous and adjacent noncancerous tissues were promptly collected and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen following surgical resection. The diagnosis of human cancers and adjacent noncancerous tissues was rigorously confirmed by independent pathologists based on histological assessments.
By the manufacturer’s instructions, paraffin-embedded samples were sliced into 4 μm thickness and immune-stained using the ZSGB-Bio Biotin Detection Kit (ZSGB-Bio, cat # SP9001, Beijing, China). Detailed procedures were outlined in
SI Appendix
.
Mouse Xenograft Studies.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Henan University. All procedures involving mice were described in
SI Appendix
.
Statistical Analysis.
A two-tailed Student's
t
test was applied to determine the statistical difference between two experimental groups. To compare more than two experimental groups, a one-way ANOVA was employed.
P
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant, and asterisks indicate the level of significance as follows: *
P
< 0.05, **
P
< 0.01, and ***
P
< 0.001. Data analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 7.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA).

body:
Lung cancer ranks as the most frequently diagnosed cancer and remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide (
1
,
2
). NSCLC constitutes approximately 85% of all lung cancer cases, and early-stage NSCLC is generally treated via surgical resection, resulting in survival rates ranging from 35% to 85%, contingent upon the tumor stage (
1
,
3
). In recent years, specific factors, such as kinase signaling pathway-related components, have been the focus of targeted therapies for lung cancer. However, there is a need to identify novel drug targets that offer alternative avenues for NSCLC-targeted treatments (
4
). Therefore, it is imperative to understand the molecular mechanism of lung cancer and discover new potential drug targets.
Posttranslational modifications (PTMs) play crucial roles in regulating cellular signal transduction during tumor progression (
5
,
6
). Among these, lysine methylation is a well-recognized PTM (
7
). Methylation of lysine residues in nonhistone proteins involves various molecular processes, including protein–protein interactions, stabilization, subcellular localization, and modifications (
8
–
11
). The activation of p38α is crucial for cell proliferation, migration, and adhesion in several cancers, including colon cancer, breast cancer, and lung cancer (
12
–
15
). The active state of p38α is tightly controlled by the MAPK signaling pathway through phosphorylation. Several PTMs of p38α, which regulate its activation, have been identified in cancer. For example, the phosphorylation of p38α at Thr180/Tyr182 is essential for its activation (
16
). Additionally, the acetylation of p38α at K53 enhances its activity by promoting ATP binding (
17
). Recent research has indicated that lysine residues in p38α undergo methylation by the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) methyltransferase (
18
). However, the demethylases involved in regulating the activation and kinase activity of p38α remain largely unidentified.
Lysine methylation is a reversible modification that is dynamically regulated by protein lysine methyltransferases (PKMTs) and protein lysine demethylases (PKDMs) (
19
). Accumulating evidence indicates that PKMTs and PKDMs drive malignant transformation through histone lysine methylation (
20
–
22
). Although lysine methylation on histone is well established, recent studies have revealed pivotal role of lysine methylation on nonhistone proteins involved in cellular processes, including tumor progression (
23
,
24
). The significance of p38α methylation in NSCLC remains to be fully elucidated. The present study identified KDM5D (also known as JARID1D and SMCY), an interacting protein of p38α, as a demethylase capable of removing methyl groups from p38α at K165.
Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database and preliminary data have indicated that KDM5D exhibits low expression in NSCLC and that high KDM5D expression is positively associated with lung cancer survival rates. However, the biological functions of KDM5D in lung cancer and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. The present results suggested that KDM5D could hinder lung cancer progression by inhibiting the activation of p38α through demethylation at K165. Methylation of p38α at K165 is revealed as a critical factor in lung cancer progression. The present findings reveal a significant role of KDM5D in inhibiting p38α activity, highlighting the KDM5D histone demethylase as a potential target for combating hyperactive p38α-driven tumor migration. Furthermore, the present results suggested that the methylation status of p38α at K165 could serve as a promising biomarker for lung cancer.
Results
K165 Methylation of p38α Promotes Its Phosphorylation.
P38α plays a crucial role in tumor development, and its subcellular localization and activity are primarily regulated by PTMs (
25
). To identify methylation sites on p38α, p38α was immunoprecipitated from HEK293T cells overexpressing Flag-tagged p38α. Mass spectrometry analysis identified the following four methylated lysine residues of p38α: Lys45 (K45), Lys118 (K118), Lys152 (K152), and Lys165 (K165) (
Fig. 1
A
–
C
). To determine whether these methylation sites regulate p38α phosphorylation, HEK293T cells were transfected with vectors encoding either wild-type or mutant p38α, followed by an assessment of p38α phosphorylation through immunoprecipitation (IP). The mutants involved the replacement of lysine residues at positions 45, 118, 152, or 165 with arginine, resulting in K45R, K118R, K152R, or K165R mutants, respectively. The K-to-R mutation maintains a positive charge and causes minimal structural change, thereby mimicking a nonmethylated state (
7
,
22
). The K165R p38α mutant effectively suppressed the phosphorylation of p38α at Thr180/Tyr182 (
Fig. 1
D
). K165 is located within the catalytic domain of the serine/threonine kinase (STKc) domain and highly conserved across species from
Gallus
to
Humans sapiens
(
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
A
).

To further elucidate the critical role of K165 methylation in promoting p38α phosphorylation, HEK293T cells were transfected with a vector encoding MEK3 along with either wild-type or mutant p38α. The mutants included a lysine-to-arginine substitution at position 165 (K165R) to mimic the nonmethylated state and a lysine-to-methionine substitution (K165M) to mimic the methylated state (
26
). The phosphorylation of p38α was significantly reduced in the presence of the p38α K165R mutant compared to the p38α wild-type or the p38α K165M mutant (
Fig. 1
E
). Furthermore, overexpression of the p38α K165R mutant in HEK293T cells impaired the phosphorylation of p38α following treatment with anisomycin, an inducer of p38α activation (
27
,
28
) (
Fig. 1
F
). These findings underscore the potential role of K165 methylation in facilitating p38α phosphorylation.
To further confirm the role of K165 methylation in the phosphorylation of p38α, an antibody specifically recognizing K165-methylated p38α was generated. Dot-blot analysis demonstrated that this antibody specifically recognized the p38α peptide methylated at K165 but did not react with the control, H3K4me peptide, or p38α R165me peptide (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
B
–
D
). Furthermore, IP assays confirmed the presence of methylated p38α at K165 in A549 cells, and the methylation level of p38α at K165 increased following anisomycin stimulation (
Fig. 1
G
). These results suggested that K165 methylation of p38α is positively correlated with its phosphorylation.
Inhibition of p38α Methylation Represses Its Oncogenic Function In Vitro and In Vivo.
To elucidate the function of p38α methylation at K165 in antitumor activity, A549 cells that stably overexpress either wild-type or mutant p38α using a lentiviral system were generated (p38α wild-type or mutant-overexpressing A549 cells) (
Fig. 2
A
). The p-p38α levels were elevated in cell lines that overexpressed wild-type p38α. However, p38α phosphorylation was reduced in cell lines overexpressing p38α K165R, and it was partially restored in cell lines overexpressing p38α K165M (
Fig. 2
A
and
B
). Furthermore, overexpression of wild-type p38α and p38α K165M in A549 cells significantly enhanced cell proliferation and migration, while overexpression of p38α K165R had a lesser impact (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
A–E
).

An
vivo
tumor model subcutaneously injected with cell lines overexpressing either wild-type or mutant p38α was used to evaluate the effect of p38α methylation on tumor progression. Tumors overexpressing the p38α K165R mutant had a smaller size and volume compared to those overexpressing wild-type p38α or the p38α K165M mutant (
Fig. 2
C
–
E
). In a mouse lung metastasis model generated by the intravenous injection of p38α wild-type or mutant-overexpressing A549 cells, the p38α K165R group displayed fewer metastatic loci and a lower lung weight compared to the wild-type p38α and p38α K165M groups (
Fig. 2
F
–
H
). These results demonstrated that overexpression of wild-type p38α significantly promotes tumor development, while this effect is substantially inhibited by the demethylation of p38α at K165. These findings implied that the demethylation of p38α at K165 plays a role in inhibiting the oncogenic function of p38α.
P38α Interacts with the PHD2 Domain of KDM5D.
Based on the finding that demethylation of p38α at K165 inhibited its phosphorylation and oncogenic function, the present study aimed to identify the specific demethylase responsible for this demethylation process by performing liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) to identify demethylases interacting with p38α. Among all the proteins associated with p38α, KDM5D was the only demethylase identified (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
A
and
B
and Table S2
). KDM5D is a demethylase of trimethylated histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) (
29
). To further confirm the interaction between p38α and KDM5D, an additional LC–MS/MS analysis was performed, which confirmed the physical interaction between KDM5D and p38α (MAPK14) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
C
and
D
and Table S3
). A subsequent IP experiment was performed to validate the LC–MS/MS results. As expected, the co-IP assay showed the interaction of KDM5D with p38α in HEK293T cells overexpressing Myc-tagged p38α and Flag-tagged KDM5D (
Fig. 3
A
and
B
). Furthermore, an endogenous interaction between p38α and KDM5D was also observed in NCI-H1299 cells, which were stably expressed KDM5D plasmids (KDM5D-overexpressing NCI-H1299 cells) (
Fig. 3
C
), further confirming the interaction. To elucidate the mechanism of this interaction, KDM5D mutants with various domain deletions were generated (
Fig. 3
D
), and the PHD2 domain of KDM5D was identified as essential for its interaction with p38α (
Fig. 3
E
). Together, these findings supported the conclusion that KDM5D interacts with p38α through its PHD2 domain.

KDM5D Demethylates p38α and Inhibits Its Activation.
Based on the interaction of p38α with KDM5D and the importance of p38α K165 methylation for its phosphorylation, the present study next investigated whether KDM5D mediates the demethylation of p38α at K165. Of note, A549 cells had the highest expression, whereas NCI-H1299 cells had bare expression (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
A
and
B
). To explore this further, KDM5D knockout A549 cells were generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system (KDM5D-deficient A549 cells), and western blot analysis confirmed the decreased expression (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
C
). Additionally, KDM5D plasmids were stably expressed in NCI-H1299 cells using the lentiviral system (KDM5D-overexpressing NCI-H1299 cells) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
D
). Knockout or overexpression of KDM5D did not affect the expression levels of KDM5A, KDM5B, or KDM5C (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
C
and
D
). To explore whether KDM5D induces demethylation of p38α, a co-IP assay was performed. The methylation of p38α at K165 increased in KDM5D-deficient A549 cells compared to control cells, whereas ectopic expression of KDM5D in NCI-H1299 cells resulted in a reduction in p38α methylation at K165 (
Fig. 4
A
). Furthermore, p38α phosphorylation was increased in KDM5D-deficient A549 cells compared to control cells (
Fig. 4
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
E
and
F
). However, KDM5D knockout did not alter the phosphorylation of p38β or p38γ/δ (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
G
). These findings suggested that KDM5D deficiency increases the phosphorylation of p38α. Ectopic expression of KDM5D led to a decrease in phosphorylated p38α levels without affecting total p38α protein levels (
Fig. 4
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
H
and
I
), and it did not affect the phosphorylation of p38β or p38γ/δ (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
J
). Consistent with the results obtained using HEK293T cells (
Fig. 1
G
), anisomycin stimulation of KDM5D-overexpressing NCI-H1299 cells promoted the upregulation of p38α methylation and phosphorylation (
Fig. 4
B
). Additionally, MEK3/MEK6 phosphorylation was evaluated by western blot analysis, which demonstrated that KDM5D knockout did not impact the levels of MEK3/MEK6 phosphorylation or their total protein levels (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
K
). Because KDM5D demethylates p38α, thereby inhibiting p38α phosphorylation, the present study next investigated the role of KDM5D in regulating p38α signaling and downstream targets involved in cell proliferation and migration. Western blot analysis demonstrated that KDM5D regulated the phosphorylation or expression levels of p38α targets, such as HSP27, C-Myc, N-cadherin, and MMP2 (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
L
and
M
).

After demonstrating that KDM5D demethylated p38α at K165, the present study subsequently determined the significance of the demethylation activity of KDM5D for p38α phosphorylation by overexpressing wild-type and mutant KDM5D [KDM5D
HE/AA
mutant (H477A and E479A), which lacks demethylation activity] in NCI-H1299 cells (
35
). The phosphorylation of p38α was significantly reduced in NCI-H1299 cells stably expressing wild-type KDM5D compared to those expressing KDM5D
HE/AA
(
Fig. 4
C
and
D
). Further co-IP results confirmed that KDM5D inhibited the phosphorylation of p38α, whereas overexpression of KDM5D
HE/AA
did not inhibit p38α phosphorylation (
Fig. 4
E
).
To test whether p38α K165 influences the interaction between p38α and MEK3, co-IP experiments were performed. The overexpressed wild-type p38α and p38α K165M interacted more strongly with MEK3 compared to overexpressed p38α K165R (
Fig. 4
F
). The structure of p38α consists of two lobes, namely, the smaller N-terminal lobe (N-lobe) and the larger C-terminal lobe (C-lobe). These lobes form an aperture that serves as an ATP docking site (surface comparison of active and inactive protein kinases has identified a conserved activation mechanism) (
30
). P38α K165 is located near the ATP binding site, suggesting a positive role of p38α methylation at K165 in promoting p38α phosphorylation (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S5
). To further examine the role of p38α K165 methylation on its phosphorylation, the phosphorylation of HSP27, a downstream target of the p38α pathway, was assessed (
14
,
29
). Overexpression of wild-type K165 and the K165M mutant, but not the K165R mutant, promoted HSP27 phosphorylation (
Fig. 4
G
). Together, these results suggested that KDM5D represses p38α phosphorylation in a demethylation-dependent manner.
KDM5D Significantly Inhibits Lung Cancer Progression.
Next, we explored whether KDM5D played a role in antitumor activity. KDM5D knockout significantly enhanced cell colony formation (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
A
and
B
) and promoted the migration of NSCLC cells (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
C
–
F
). Moreover, ectopic expression of KDM5D in NCI-H1299 cells exhibited an inhibitory effect on both cell proliferation and migration, confirming the antitumor activity of KDM5D (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
G
–
L
). These findings demonstrate that KDM5D can inhibit lung cancer cell colony formation and migration in vitro.
To gain deeper insights into the antitumor function of KDM5D, an in vivo transplantable model was generated by subcutaneously injecting control or KDM5D-deficient A549 cells. The body weights of mice injected with control and KDM5D-deficient A549 cells did not significantly differ (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
). However, the size, weight, and volume of tumors obtained from mice in the KDM5D knockout group were significantly larger compared to those in the control group (
Fig. 5
A
–
C
). Consistently, overexpression of KDM5D suppressed tumorigenicity in a mouse subcutaneous xenograft model compared to control cells (
Fig. 5
D
–
F
). In addition, a mouse lung metastasis model was generated by intravenously injecting control and KDM5D-deficient A549 cells. There were more tumor loci in the lungs of mice injected with KDM5D-deficient cells compared to control cells (
Fig. 5
G
and
H
). There was also a significant increase in the methylation of p38α at K165, which correlated with the observed increase in p38α phosphorylation (
Fig. 5
I
and
J
).

To validate whether the p38α MAPK signaling pathway is involved in the role of KDM5D in inhibiting tumor progression, cell migration was evaluated in both control and KDM5D-deficient A549 cells that were pretreated with SB203580, a p38α inhibitor (
31
,

P38α K165 Methylation and Cancer Progression Are Positively Correlated in Lung Cancer Tissue Specimens.
To better understand the correlation between p38α K165 methylation and the progression of lung cancer, 56 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded lung cancer specimens were examined, including 20 cases of grade I, 6 cases of grade II, 13 cases of grade III, and 17 cases of grade IV. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was utilized to assess the levels of p38α K165 methylation (

A

Discussion
The present study provides evidence that KDM5D demethylates p38α at K165 and this methylation correlates with p38α phosphorylation in NSCLC. This research uncovers a unique regulatory mechanism within the MAPK signaling pathway, mediated by lysine demethylation. The findings emphasize the importance of PTMs in nonhistone proteins and their impact on cellular processes and tumorigenesis. By demonstrating that KDM5D acts as a tumor suppressor through its demethylase activity, this study opens broad avenues for targeted NSCLC therapies, specifically focusing on the demethylation of p38α.
PTMs play a critical role in regulating the signal transduction of the p38 MAP kinase pathway in various biological and pathological processes. For example, activating p38α via protein arginine methylation on R49/R149 by PRMT1 promotes erythroid differentiation (
34
). Additionally, PRMT7 methylates p38α at the R70 residue, promoting myoblast differentiation (
35
). In addition to arginine methylation, lysine methylation of nonhistone proteins has also emerged as a critical regulatory mechanism in cancer biology. Recent studies have reported that EZH2 methylates p38α at lysine residues, enhancing its stability and function (
18
). The present study demonstrated that KDM5D-mediated demethylation of p38α at K165 inhibits its phosphorylation and subsequent activation, thus impairing its oncogenic functions both in vitro and in vivo. This mechanism highlights a layer of complexity in the regulation of the p38α MAPK pathway, which is vital for cell proliferation, migration, and survival in various cancers. The present findings provide insights into how the modification of specific lysine residues influence protein function and cellular behavior.
Although previous reports have highlighted the role of KDM5 family demethylases in cancer (
36
–
41
), the specific role of KDM5D, the least studied isoform within the KDM5 family, in tumor progression remains unknown. Among H3K4 methyltransferases and demethylases, KDM5D is male-specific due to its localization on the Y chromosome (
42
). Loss of the Y chromosome has been associated with the downregulation of KDM5D epigenetic modifiers in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC) (
43
). A recent study has also suggested that KDM5D may function as an epigenetic repressor, primarily influencing the invasion, rather than the proliferation, of prostate cancer cells (
44
). Another report has indicated that deletion of KDM5D may lead to enhanced survival, resulting in progression beyond cell-cycle arrest and DNA replication stress. These varying findings suggest that KDM5D may play a role in cell proliferation by regulating the cell cycle in aggressive prostate tumor cells (
45
). Given this existing controversy, the present study aimed to elucidate the roles of KDM5D in NSCLC. The present data indicate that KDM5D inhibits both the proliferation and migration of NSCLC cells by demethylating p38α, which prevents activation of p38α, suggesting a broader tumor-suppressive role for KDM5D than previously recognized. This finding is consistent with earlier reports that have identified KDM5D as a tumor suppressor due to its downregulation, mutation, or loss in prostate cancer (
43
) and CCRCC (
42
). Furthermore, recent research has revealed that Y chromosome loss drives more aggressive tumor growth and is associated with a poorer prognosis in bladder cancer (
38
). Given its lower expression in NSCLC tissues and its positive correlation with patient survival, KDM5D represents a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target.
KDM5D, similar to other members of the KDM5 family, can demethylate H3K4me3 (
29
). Most previous studies have primarily focused on the regulation of gene expression related to cell cycle control, cell proliferation, and apoptosis through histone methylation. However, emerging research indicates that histone methylation modifiers can impact a wide array of molecular events, including protein–protein interactions, protein stability, subcellular localization, and protein modifications, by regulating the methylation of nonhistone substrates (
23
,
46
,
47
). For example, the KDM2A histone H3 lysine 36 (H3K36) demethylase promotes lung tumorigenesis by enhancing ERK1/2 signaling via epigenetic mechanisms (
48
). Similarly, SETDB1-mediated Akt methylation is up-regulated and associated with Akt hyperactivation in NSCLC, contributing to tumor development. Based on these studies, the present study investigated whether p38α serves as a nonhistone substrate for histone demethylases and whether methylation of p38α plays a pivotal role in MAPK signaling and tumor progression. The present study successfully identified p38α as a nonhistone substrate of KDM5D and demonstrates that KDM5D-mediated demethylation of p38α at K165 contributes to the dephosphorylation of p38α. This research has enhanced the knowledge of the substrates and functions of KDM5D, a gene that is often down-regulated in lung cancer. Further research is needed to understand the precise mechanisms involved.
The down-regulation of KDM5D has been linked to an unfavorable survival outcome in males (
49
). A previous study has indicated that the incidence of LUAD is lower in males than in females (
50
). Given that the present analysis of TCGA database revealed minimal KDM5D expression in the lungs of healthy females, the female predisposition to LUAD may be linked to the absence of KDM5D expression. Due to advancements in early lung cancer diagnosis, the availability of fresh lung cancer tumor samples is relatively limited. As the result, the sample size was limited in the present study (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
H
). The present analysis suggested that the reduced KDM5D expression is often associated with elevated p38α methylation and p38α phosphorylation (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
H
and
I
). However, the correlation between KDM5D expression and increased p38α methylation and phosphorylation is not observed in some human lung tumors, suggesting contribution of other factors, which will be investigated in the future.
In summary, the present findings highlighted the significant antitumor effect of KDM5D primarily through inactivating p38α. The ability of KDM5D to demethylate p38α at K165 can contribute to regulating p38α activation through down-regulating p38α phosphorylation, thereby influencing cancer progression. This p38α methylation event also serves as an adverse prognostic indicator for NSCLC patients. Further, targeting KDM5D-mediated p38α K165 demethylation emerges as a promising therapeutic strategy for NSCLC.
Materials and Methods
Cell Lines and Cell Culture.
The HEK293T, A549, and BEAS-2B (a human bronchial epithelial cell line) were cultured at 37 °C in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 50 mg/mL penicillin/streptomycin in a humidified incubator with 5% CO
2
. The NCI-H1299, NCI-H1373, and NCI-H1573 cells were cultured at 37 °C in 1640 complete medium containing 10% FBS and 50 mg/mL penicillin/streptomycin. These cells were used within 10 to 15 passages. Cell culture reagents and other chemicals were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Gibco & Hyclone) and Sigma-Aldrich.
Reagents and Antibodies.
Most biochemical reagents were purchased from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). All the special reagents and antibodies can be found in
SI Appendix
.
Plasmid Constructs and Transfection.
The lentiviruses for CRISPR/Cas9-based editing of KDM5D were generated as previously described (
22
). All plasmids were sequenced and confirmed for accuracy. More details were found in
SI Appendix
. The sequences of PCR primers for Expressing Vectors used in this study are listed in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
.
Survival Analysis and Gene Expression Analysis.
KDM5D expression data were obtained from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (
7
,
24
,
25
). Additionally, for survival analysis, a publicly accessible transcriptomic dataset for lung cancer was utilized (
https://kmplot.com/analysis
) (
7
,
26
,
27
).
Mass Spectrometry Analyses.
For mass spectrometry analysis aimed at identifying methylation sites, anti-Flag IPs were conducted using whole cell lysates (WCLs) obtained from three 10-cm dishes of HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-p38α. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated via SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. All gel bands were excised and subjected to reverse-phase nanospray liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (Analytical Instrumentation Center of PEKING University, Beijing, China).
LC–MS/MS analysis was conducted to identify proteins interacting with p38α. A co-IP was performed using WCLs from HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-p38α or an empty vector control. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE, and Coomassie staining was used for visualization. All the gel bands were excised and subsequently subjected to LC–MS/MS (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
B
) (Beijing Protein Innovation, China). Additionally, LC–MS/MS was employed to identify proteins interacting with KDM5D. Co-IP was performed using WCLs in HEK293T cells transfected with Flag-KDM5D or an empty vector control. The immunoprecipitated proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and subjected to Coomassie staining. All bands were excised and subjected to LC–MS/MS (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
D
) (Beijing Protein Innovation, China).
qRT-PCR Analysis.
Total RNA was isolated using the RNAeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen). After quantifying using a Nanodrop 1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific), one microgram of total RNA was reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA with a Superscript III kit (Invitrogen). Real-time PCR was performed using the Power SYBR green PCR master mix (Takara). All analyses were performed using an Applied Biosystems® 7500 Fast PCR machine. mRNA was normalized by GAPDH. Each experiment was performed in triplicate.
Western Blot and Immunoprecipitation.
Methods of western blot and IP were described in
SI Appendix
.
Colony Formation Assays.
Cells were seeded into 6-well plates (500 cells/well) and incubated for 8 to 14 d until visible colonies formed. The colonies were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and fixed with 4% PFA for 20 min, then stained with 0.4% crystal violet in 20% ethanol for 30 min. After staining, the plates were washed, air-dried, and the number of colonies was counted. The control or KDM5D-deficient cells were treated with the p38α MAPK inhibitor SB203580 (10 μM, Selleck, cat # S1076) for 12 h prior to the colony formation assay.
Transwell Migration Assay.
A total of 5 × 10
4
cells were seeded on the porous membrane of each insert for the transwell migration assay. A more detailed method was described in
SI Appendix
.
Wound-Healing Assay.
A total of 7 × 10
5
A549 cells or 5 × 10
5
NCI-H1299 cells were seeded in a well of a 6-well plate, and a more detailed method was described in
SI Appendix
.
IHC staining.
This study was granted approval from the Institutional Review Board at the First Affiliated Hospital of Henan University. Informed consent was duly obtained from all patients who participated in this study. Paired fresh cancerous and adjacent noncancerous tissues were promptly collected and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen following surgical resection. The diagnosis of human cancers and adjacent noncancerous tissues was rigorously confirmed by independent pathologists based on histological assessments.
By the manufacturer’s instructions, paraffin-embedded samples were sliced into 4 μm thickness and immune-stained using the ZSGB-Bio Biotin Detection Kit (ZSGB-Bio, cat # SP9001, Beijing, China). Detailed procedures were outlined in
SI Appendix
.
Mouse Xenograft Studies.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Henan University. All procedures involving mice were described in
